strengths: Novel and unique dataset: GIQ is the first benchmark, to my knowledge, combining systematically rendered synthetic polyhedra (224 shapes spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, stellations, Kepler-Poinsot, compounds, and nonconvex uniform classes) with real physical paper models photographed in the wild — a substantial curation effort with unambiguous ground-truth geometry and symmetry annotations.

Well-motivated evaluation design: the four experimental paradigms (monocular reconstruction, 3D symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot classification) probe geometric intelligence at different levels, connecting to established cognitive-science instruments (MRT) and prior probing literature.

Useful empirical findings: linear probing reveals DINOv2 encodes 3D symmetry elements surprisingly well (up to 93% on wild images), while hard-split MRT shows near-chance generalization from synthetic to real imagery — a clear, actionable contrast; the qualitative analysis of frontier VLM errors (misjudging convexity, face geometry, compound structure) is informative and well-presented.
Controlled synthetic rendering pipeline (Mitsuba, uniform viewpoints, constrained lighting) supports systematic synthetic-to-wild generalization analysis with train-on-synthetic/test-on-wild splits.
weaknesses: The monocular 3D reconstruction evaluation is weak: only three shapes (cube, great dodecahedron, small cubicuboctahedron) and three methods, reported qualitatively via rendered images in Table 2 with no quantitative metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score). Claims that 'state-of-the-art reconstruction algorithms struggle to reconstruct even Bearer [REDACTED] forms' are thus anecdotal rather than rigorously supported.

Limited model coverage and somewhat dated models: only Shap-E, Stable Fast 3D, and OpenLRM for reconstruction; no newer feedforward reconstructors or optimization-based baselines (e.g., SDFit-like approaches or analysis-by-synthesis) that might actually succeed on clean polyhedra, leaving open whether the reported failures reflect fundamental limits or simply the choice of models.

Scale of the dataset is modest (224 shapes, ~40 images each), and several experimental details are deferred to supplementary material, making it hard to judge test-set sizes and statistical significance; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported anywhere.

Presentation flaws: incomplete sentences (Sec. 3.4 'constructed by .' appears to be missing a reference/attribution; 'differing only by rotation. . Such a scenario'), abstract says 'publicly available here' with no link, and citation [50]/[51] for SAM is incorrect (those are the SAM optimizer and a ViT paper, not the Segment Anything Model).

The symmetry-detection task covers only three symmetry elements; the MRT 'hard split' pairs appear manually selected without documented selection criteria or size, raising concerns about reproducibility of the headline negative result (near-chance accuracy).

Limited insight into why models fail: no ablations (e.g., viewpoint coverage, texture, background) or human baselines on the wild tasks, so the benchmark establishes gaps but provides limited diagnostic value beyond the qualitative VLM error analysis.

strengths: The GIQ dataset is genuinely novel and unique: 224 carefully curated polyhedra spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, Kepler-Poinsot, and nonconvex uniform solids, with both synthetic Mitsuba renderings and real physical paper models photographed in controlled and in-the-wild conditions. I am not aware of another resource with this combination of precise geometric ground truth (symmetry groups, convexity, complexity hierarchy) and real-world imagery.

The paper targets a real and timely gap: existing 3D probing studies (e.g., El Banani et al., Lexicon3D) rely on datasets like OmniObject3D/NAVI/GSO that lack fine-grained geometric annotations, so a benchmark with unambiguous ground truth on symmetry and shape class is a useful community contribution.

The four evaluation paradigms (reconstruction, symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot VLM classification) probe complementary levels of geometric ability, and the qualitative error analysis of frontier VLM responses (Table 3b) is insightful, revealing systematic failures in convexity, face-geometry, and compound-structure reasoning.
The writing is generally clear, and the connection to cognitive science (MRT, symmetry perception) is well motivated.
weaknesses: The monocular reconstruction evaluation (Sec. 4.1) is very weak: only three models (Shap-E, Stable Fast 3D, OpenLRM) are tested on only three shape categories, with purely qualitative results (Table 2). No quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, F-score, IoU) are reported, no confidence or aggregate statistics over the 224 shapes, and no discussion of why these three shapes are representative. Conclusions like 'all three models exhibited significant reconstruction failures for most tested cases' are not supported by the evidence shown.

The symmetry-detection result (DINOv2 achieving 0.85-0.97 balanced accuracy) may reflect shortcut learning: single-view silhouette/shading cues correlate strongly with rotational symmetry in this dataset, and the paper provides no analysis (e.g., probing on masked/silhouette-only inputs) to establish that the embeddings genuinely capture 3D structure rather than 2D regularities. The strong claim that 'DINOv2's image embeddings inherently capture fundamental 3D structural properties' is therefore not well supported.

The mental rotation test results are underdeveloped: models are only evaluated via linear probes on embedding differences, no VLMs are included in MRT despite them being the focus of Sec. 4.4, the 'hard' split pair construction is only exemplified with six pairs (Table 4), and the Syn-Wild condition conflates shape matching with a severe synthetic-to-real domain gap, making the 'near chance' result hard to interpret as a failure of geometric reasoning per se.

The zero-shot classification task is partially a memorization/lookup test (naming obscure polyhedra like Wenninger models), which frontier models can partially solve via textual recall rather than geometric reasoning; only aggregate accuracies are shown with no per-class variance, prompt sensitivity analysis, or human baseline.

There are apparent factual/technical errors that undermine rigor: (a) Sec. 3.2 states Catalan solids 'retain vertex uniformity of the dual,' directly contradicting Table 1 ('face-transitive, but not vertex-transitive') - Catalan solids are face-transitive, not vertex-uniform; (b) references [50, 51] cited for SAM are actually the SAM optimizer and deit-iii-related training papers, not the Segment Anything paper; (c) Llama is listed as a 'foundation vision model'; (d) a citation is visibly broken in Sec. 3.4 ('constructed by .').

No analytical depth is offered beyond headline results: no ablations on probe layer choice, no error analysis on symmetry probing, no investigation of view-dependence, and limited discussion of how the uniform yellowish diffuse rendering and background-removal preprocessing may artificially simplify or confound the tasks.

Several presentation issues remain: incomplete sentences ('differing only by rotation. .'), key details (dataset composition, splits, supplementary figures) deferred to supplementary material without in-paper summaries, and Table 1 notes the categorization is 'arbitrary' without justifying why this taxonomy supports the claims.

Significance is bounded: the benchmark covers a narrow object class (polyhedra), and while the paper argues this enables precise ground truth, it is unclear how findings generalize to everyday 3D objects; there is also no demonstration that the benchmark can diagnose or improve models (e.g., fine-tuning or data-augmentation experiments), limiting its stated utility as a 'diagnostic tool'.

strengths: Novel and unique benchmark contribution: GIQ is the first dataset combining a systematic taxonomy of 224 polyhedra (Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, stellations, compounds, uniform non-convex) with both physically-based synthetic renderings and real photographs of hand-built paper models, providing unambiguous ground truth for symmetry, convexity, and complexity that existing 3D datasets (Objaverse, OmniObject3D, NAVI, GSO) lack.

Multi-faceted evaluation design covering four complementary paradigms (monocular reconstruction, 3D symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot VLM classification), probing geometric intelligence at different levels from implicit features to high-level language-model reasoning.

Interesting and well-supported findings: the result that DINOv2 linear probes achieve up to 93% on wild images for 4-fold rotational symmetry without 3D supervision is a notable positive insight, while the near-chance Syn-Wild mental rotation and systematic VLM failure modes (convexity confusion, compound misinterpretation, ignored color-coded cues) are clearly documented with qualitative error analysis.

The real-world (wild) image collection, including physically constructed non-convex models photographed across varied conditions, is a substantial and unusual data collection effort that enables genuine synthetic-to-real generalization testing.
Clear motivation and positioning relative to cognitive science literature (Mental Rotation Test, symmetry perception) and to prior probing work (El Banani et al., Lexicon3d).
weaknesses: The monocular 3D reconstruction evaluation is very narrow: only three shape categories (cube, great dodecahedron, small cubicuboctahedron) and purely qualitative renderings in Table 2, with no quantitative metrics (Chamfer distance, F-score, IoU). The strong claim that SOTA methods 'struggle to reconstruct even Bearer [REDACTED] forms' rests on a very small and selectively chosen sample.

Statistical rigor is lacking throughout: no confidence intervals or significance tests for the symmetry probing and MRT results; the hard MRT split appears small (six example pairs are shown) and the 'hard' pair selection is manual without defined criteria, raising concerns about cherry-picking and generalization of the near-chance conclusion.

The zero-shot VLM classification uses a single minimal prompt ('What is the name of this polyhedron?'), conflating knowledge of obscure nomenclature (e.g., Johnson solid names) with geometric reasoning; no prompt ablations, no controlled evaluation of geometric property questions, and no human baseline despite claims that the distinctions are 'readily apparent to humans'.

Several reproducibility and completeness issues: the dataset link is a placeholder ('available here'), the wild-image section has an incomplete sentence ('constructed by .'), the test-split composition details are deferred entirely to supplementary material, and the SAM citation [50, 51] appears incorrect (referencing SAM optimization papers rather than the Segment Anything model).

Scope of conclusions versus evidence: sweeping claims about 'geometric intelligence' of foundation models are drawn from relatively few tasks, few shapes per task (e.g., 26 unseen shapes for symmetry probing), and models trained only on synthetic data for wild evaluation, without disentangling domain shift from geometric reasoning failure.

The paper is primarily an empirical study with no methodological contribution or analysis of why models fail (e.g., no exploration of whether failures stem from texture bias, viewpoint ambiguity, or feature geometry), limiting its actionable impact.

strengths: Novel and well-motivated benchmark: GIQ is the first dataset of its kind targeting 3D geometric reasoning with polyhedra, whose well-defined symmetry groups and complexity hierarchy provide unambiguous ground truth — a genuine gap compared to prior object datasets (OmniObject3D, NAVI, GSO).

Impressive dataset construction effort: 224 unique shapes spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, Kepler-Poinsot, stellation, and compound classes, with both physically-based synthetic renderings (Mitsuba) and real paper models photographed in the wild — the synthetic/wild pairing enables meaningful sim-to-real evaluation.

Breadth of evaluation: four complementary task suites (monocular 3D reconstruction, 3D symmetry detection, mental rotation, zero-shot classification) probing explicit reconstruction, implicit representations, and high-level semantic reasoning across a broad set of encoders (CLIP, DINOv2, SAM, VGGT, DUSt3R, MASt3R, etc.) and frontier VLMs.
Human baseline study (42 participants) on the MRT task is a valuable addition that grounds model performance against human perception, showing most humans still outperform the best model.

Systematic methodology: careful handling of class imbalance, cross-validation with unseen-shape folds, synonym accounting for VLM classification, CoT and multi-view ablations, and inclusion of geometry-native 3D models (ShapeLLM, PointLLM) to test whether limitations are architecture-specific.
Insightful qualitative error analysis of frontier model failures (convexity confusion, conflating compounds/stellations, hallucinated face types), which is useful for future work.
weaknesses: Limited quantitative rigor in the reconstruction evaluation: only 3 representative shapes are tested and Table 1 is essentially qualitative; no standard 3D metrics (Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score) are reported in the main text, making the claim that 'state-of-the-art reconstruction fails even on Platonic solids' difficult to verify from the paper itself.

The zero-shot classification task partially conflates geometric reasoning with terminology recall: 'perfect' accuracy of Gemini on Kepler-Poinsot solids suggests memorization of rare named shapes rather than geometric understanding, and the paper does not adequately separate these factors.

Sample sizes for several evaluations are small (e.g., 3 shapes for reconstruction, 20 hard-split MRT questions per participant, 25 questions in the human study), which limits statistical power for some of the headline claims; error bars are largely absent.

Several presentational and citation issues undermine polish: references like SAM are misattributed (Foret et al. 2020 is SAM optimizer, not Segment Anything), an author/citation blank remains in Sec. 3.4 ('constructed by —'), the public URL is missing in the abstract, and there are grammatical errors (e.g., 'we used the GIQ dataset to conducted').

Renderings at 256×256 with diffuse-only shading and no texture/color variation may oversimplify the visual statistics compared to real-world imagery; impact of these rendering choices on conclusions is not ablated.

Novelty is solid but incremental in framing: the paper extends existing probing/mental-rotation methodology (El Banani et al., Ramakrishnan et al.) to a new shape domain rather than introducing new techniques; significance depends heavily on community adoption of the benchmark.
Some claims, such as 'models failing GIQ are unprepared for the geometric calculus of complex scenes,' are speculative and unsupported by any correlation analysis with downstream task performance.

strengths: The paper targets an interesting and underexplored question: how well do vision foundation models, monocular 3D reconstruction methods, and frontier VLMs reason about precise 3D geometric properties, using polyhedra whose symmetry groups and complexity provide unambiguous ground truth.

The dataset combines synthetic renderings (Mitsuba) with real physical paper models photographed in the wild, which is a genuinely distinctive and labor-intensive asset; the accompanying meshes enable controlled probing.

Evaluation spans multiple complementary dimensions (reconstruction, symmetry probing, mental rotation, zero-shot classification) across a broad and current set of models (DINOv2, SigLIP, SAM, VGGT, DUSt3R, MASt3R, o3, Gemini 2.5, Claude 3.7, geometry-native VLMs).

The inclusion of a human baseline with a 42-participant user study, showing that most humans outperform the best model on the hard mental rotation split, adds a useful reference point often missing in probing studies.
The qualitative error analysis of frontier VLM failures (confusing convexity, conflating compounds with stellations, hallucinating face types) is informative and well illustrated.
weaknesses: The monocular 3D reconstruction evaluation is weak and largely anecdotal: only three shapes (cube, great dodecahedron, small cubicuboctahedron) are tested, and 'Table 1' is purely qualitative image visualizations. There are no quantitative metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score) despite ground-truth meshes being available, making the central claim that 'state-of-the-art reconstruction fails on Platonic solids' under-supported.

Several central findings rest on very small or ambiguous evidence. For example, 'Gemini 2.5 Pro achieved perfect accuracy for Kepler-Poinsot solids' sits awkwardly with the narrative that all models struggle; per-category results are pushed to the appendix and the main text cherry-picks highlights.

The zero-shot VLM classification experiment has a serious contamination/interpretability confound that is acknowledged only in passing: frontier models can recall canonical polyhedra names (e.g., via parametric knowledge or tool use, as when Gemini explicitly performs a Google search during the query). This conflates 'geometric reasoning' with retrieval of shape names, weakening the claim of a 'geometric reasoning gap.'

The benchmark's novelty relative to prior work is limited: mental rotation evaluation with VLMs exists (Ramakrishnan et al., 2024) and 3D-awareness probing is well established (El Banani et al., 2024; Man et al., 2024); the contribution is mainly a new shape set plus adapted tasks, which is modest.

The paper is sloppy and incomplete in multiple places: the entity that constructed the physical models is left blank ('constructed by —'), the public URL in the abstract is missing, there are duplicated periods and grammatical errors ('We used the GIQ dataset to conducted'), and citation errors (SAM attributed to Foret et al. 2020, which is the SAMM optimizer; inconsistent Boss et al. 2024/2025 for SF3D). For a dataset/benchmark paper whose value depends on release quality, these are significant red flags.

The dataset is small (224 shapes) and coverage decisions appear somewhat ad hoc (a 'representative subset of 48 Johnson solids'; a self-described 'arbitrary' categorization in Fig. 2), limiting generalization of conclusions about 'geometric intelligence' as a whole.

The ambitious framing ('geometric litmus test', 'models failing GIQ are unprepared for geometric calculus of complex scenes') is speculative and not empirically substantiated; no evidence is provided that GIQ scores correlate with performance on real-world 3D tasks.

Reproducibility concerns: model versions of closed-source APIs (o3, o4-mini-high, Gemini 2.5 Pro, Claude 3.7) change rapidly, making classification results hard to reproduce; no protocol is given for controlling tool use (search), which we know from their own qualitative example materially affects results.

Human study design details are thin (42 participants, 25 questions, 30s limit); accuracy is measured on a small subset, and comparisons of '68% of participants outperformed the best model' involve few items per participant, making the comparison noisy.

strengths: GIQ is a genuinely novel and carefully curated resource: 224 unique polyhedra spanning Platonic, Archimedean, Catalan, Johnson, Kepler-Poinsot, stellation, and compound families, instantiated in both high-quality physically-based synthetic renderings (Mitsuba) and an impressive set of physically constructed paper models photographed in the wild. This combination of mathematically precise ground truth with real-world variability is rare and provides unambiguous supervision for geometric evaluations.

The paper evaluates a broad and well-chosen spectrum of models: 12+ image encoders (supervised, self-supervised, multi-view/geometry-native like VGGT/DUSt3R/MASt3R), three monocular reconstruction methods, four frontier VLMs (Claude, Gemini, ChatGPT o3/o4-mini), and 3D-native LLMs (ShapeLLM, PointLLM, LLaVA-3D), enabling cross-paradigm comparisons rarely seen in one work.

Methodologically sound experimental design in several places: 5-fold cross-validation with shape-disjoint splits for symmetry probing, class-imbalance handling with weighted loss and balanced accuracy, non-linear probe controls, explicit exclusion of ambiguous Johnson solids, synonym dictionaries for VLM classification, and CoT/multi-view ablations to rule out prompting artifacts.

The inclusion of a 42-participant human baseline with a calibrated hard/easy split and time limits is a strong contribution; anchoring model performance to human data (top humans at 90% vs. best model ~69%) makes the 'gap' claims concrete rather than anecdotal.

The qualitative error analysis of frontier VLMs (confusing convexity, conflating compounds with stellations, hallucinating face types) is insightful and clearly demonstrates systematic geometric misinterpretation rather than mere naming failures, and the 'geometric litmus test' framing is compelling.
weaknesses: The monocular 3D reconstruction evaluation is strikingly narrow: only three shapes (cube, great dodecahedron, small cubicuboctahedron) are evaluated, with results presented primarily as a qualitative figure (Table 1). Sweeping claims that 'reconstruction is unreliable even for Platonic solids' rest on a tiny, hand-picked sample without quantitative metrics (e.g., Chamfer distance, IoU, F-score) over the full 224-shape corpus. This is the weakest section of the paper.

Zero-shot classification by exact polyhedron name partially measures taxonomic/terminology knowledge rather than geometric reasoning: a model might correctly perceive face counts and symmetry yet fail to retrieve the obscure name of a Johnson or uniform non-convex solid. The paper should disentangle naming recall from geometric perception (e.g., verification-style tasks: 'is this convex?', 'how many faces?', 'which of these two shapes is this?').

The dataset is small in a critical sense: 224 unique shapes with ~40 images each yields limited diversity for probe generalization, and the accuracy differences among encoders in Figure 3 (left) appear within plausible variance ranges; no confidence intervals or significance tests are reported for the cross-encoder comparisons.

The paper contains several incomplete or garbled passages: the constructor of the paper models is unnamed ('constructed by —'), the dataset URL in the abstract is missing/broken, stray double periods ('(72°) symmetries. .'), and 'to conducted a series' — issues suggesting a rushed submission, which is concerning for reproducibility of the data-release claims.

Apparent inconsistencies: Boss et al. cited as both 2024 and 2025 for SF3D, and He & Wang 2023 vs. Hong et al. 2024 for OpenLRM/LRM; SAM is cited via Foret et al. (2020) which is the SAM paper's neighbor (Sharpness-Aware Minimization), an apparent citation error.

The abstract's framing of 'remarkably low accuracy' for VLMs is somewhat at odds with the results (perfect scores on Platonic and Kepler-Poinsot solids by some models); claims should be calibrated per-category.

The human study, while valuable, uses a 30-second limit per question and a small participant pool; human-to-model comparability (and the claim that '68% of participants outperformed the best model') would benefit from more detail on participant expertise and analysis of per-item difficulty.

Positioning relative to concurrent spatial-reasoning benchmarks (e.g., VSI-Bench, BLINK, RAM-based MRT studies) is thin; a more rigorous comparison of what GIQ uniquely measures versus these existing suites would strengthen the contribution claim.
